title: Dockside repair work and a reserve held from final wages
narrative:
This is an authored maritime-services scenario concerning a fictional dockside repair team.

An adult technician has spent five weeks repairing cargo equipment while a vessel remains in port. The technician works for a shore-based subcontractor rather than the vessel operator. Another company arranged accommodation and an induction course. The technician's file contains three business names and no document explaining which company is responsible for a disputed reserve against future travel costs.

The employment offer describes weekly wages. Three weeks were paid normally. The next statement shows an amount labelled repatriation reserve, but gives neither a balance held nor a release date. The technician has asked whether this represents money already taken from earned pay, a proposed future deduction or an accounting note. A supervisor says reserves are standard in the sector. That description alone does not establish the applicable rule, the proper payer or the worker's consent.

Access to part of the dock is limited during crane movements. Security records show that everyone uses a marked alternative walkway during those periods. The technician has gone ashore for groceries after work and keeps the original travel document. Those facts help separate a specific safety arrangement from any claim that the worker cannot stop working. The latest replies below concern that employment choice directly.

The repair schedule has slipped because replacement parts arrived late. The vessel operator would like the same team to stay for another fortnight, and the subcontractor says it would be expensive to train replacements. The technician is considering an extension, but only after understanding pay and being able to decline. A return ticket has not yet been purchased. No one should assume the technician has a guaranteed job or travel arrangement waiting elsewhere.

A colleague believes the reserve is an insurance requirement; another says it protects the subcontractor from workers leaving early. Neither has supplied an insurance policy or wage instruction. The technician wants a confidential explanation before a dispute is raised with the vessel operator. They are willing to share the payslips with an independent adviser but have not authorized broader circulation among the companies.

[MR-R1] Payroll reply: "The final earnings have been retained. We will release them only if you accept the two-week extension or pay the reserve account yourself."

[MR-R2] Supervisor message: "Your request to end the assignment is refused. If you take this to an outside adviser, we will remove your name from future work lists." The technician says the unpaid money is needed for ordinary living costs.

[MR-R3] Access account: "I keep my original travel document and go ashore after work using the available walkway."
